title: Skill and Will
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece offers a simple two-factor framework for diagnosing team member performance: skill and will. The author argues results are the clearest evidence of skill, and that leaders should be honest about whether coaching can close a skill gap. Will is treated as the harder, more personal variable, something leaders can rarely instill in someone who doesn't already have it. The piece's practical suggestion is a periodic two-dimensional review of every team member against skill and will.
points: Performance can be diagnosed along two simple axes, skill and will, and most chronic underperformance traces back to a deficit in one or both.
Results are the clearest evidence of skill; leaders should honestly assess whether coaching can close a skill gap.
Will is framed as largely outside a leader's control, most attempts to motivate someone who lacks internal drive are described as a losing effort.
The piece recommends a periodic, explicit skill-and-will review of every team member as a diagnostic habit.
quotes: We can boil down the lengthy list of positive and negative attributes into two common-sense factors: Skill and Will.
Results speak the loudest when deciding who on the team is the most skillful. The proof is always in the pudding when it comes to skill.
While many leaders believe they can motivate team members who lack the desire to achieve, most often this is a losing effort. The will to achieve is something only the team member controls.
When evaluating the reason for consistently poor performance by a given team member, leaders might be surprised at how often it comes down to these two foundational qualities.
Who on your team has the skill and the will? And who doesn’t? Make this simple assessment. You’ll know what to do.
